title: The joy of the Lord (Nehemiah 8:1–12)
hookLine: the law is read aloud and people weep; go, eat, share, the joy of the Lord is your strength
last: LET US RISE UP AND BUILD.

lines: THE SQUARE BY THE WATER GATE.
HE OPENS THE BOOK; THEY STAND.
cards: The wall is finished, and the people gather inside it, but not for a parade. In the open square by the Water Gate, men and women and everyone old enough to understand ask Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of the law.

He climbs onto a wooden platform built for the day, high enough for the whole crowd to see. He opens the book, and the moment he does, the people stand. Then he reads, from early morning until midday.
Remember the lost book, found in the temple and read first to a king? This time the people themselves ask for it.

teach.b: Ezra blesses the Lord, and "all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands."

The Levites, the teachers, help the people understand: "they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." And once the people understand, it breaks them.
"All the people wept, when they heard the words of the law." The text doesn't say why. Some readers hear grief at how far the people had wandered, like Josiah tearing his clothes.
Then Nehemiah, Ezra and the teachers stop the weeping.

Not because grief is wrong, but because of what day it is: "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."
Look at the order: eat, drink, send some to the people with nothing ready, and then the reason. And notice whose joy it is: the joy of the Lord. It isn't a mood anyone is told to manufacture.

It holds people up, and it comes out as a shared meal. The chapter ends with the people going off to eat, drink, send portions and make great mirth, "because they had understood the words that were declared unto them."
Understanding led to tears first, then to a feast.

how: Some Christians quote Nehemiah 8:10, the joy of the LORD is your strength, in hard seasons, and some churches end a time of confession or lament with a shared meal in the same spirit.

games.q: you're a leader in the square. the law has been read and the whole crowd is weeping. what do you tell them?
o: go, eat, drink, and send portions to those with nothing.
go home quietly and think about it.
games.why: "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared... for the joy of the LORD is your strength."

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been heavy about lately.
Then turn toward a table: something sweet or rich, and someone for whom nothing is prepared, someone eating alone, someone new, someone who's had a hard week, and picture handing it to them.
If you pray, thank God for the food you'd share; if you don't, just let the picture warm you.

wordCard.voice: Ezra. The scribe who read the law aloud until the people wept, then told them: go, eat, drink, and send portions to those with nothing ready, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.

orig.note: Hebrew: the joy of the LORD (Nehemiah 8:10). Jewish readers say Adonai in place of the divine name.

carryVoice: Your line: joy is your strength. It comes to the table, and it's meant to be shared. Day seven hundred forty-three, complete.
